doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: European recordings and return to America
title: Electronic Sonata and Othello: the albums and their labels
summary: Russell describes Electronic Sonata made in Swedish Radio's electronic studio and the Norwegian Radio Othello ballet, while Daughtry sorts out the Flying Dutchman and Strata-East labels.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: We were talking about recordings and about the music of course as we work our way through your time in Europe during the ’60s. Late in the ’60s I recall two recordings. Actually, I recall them from the early ’70s, when I encountered them, but I believe they’re from the late ’60s. One is called The Othello Ballet Suite and the other is called Electronic Sonata for Souls Loved by Nature. Those are incredible recordings and very, very important in music, in world music. Can you tell us a little bit about them, what was behind them, the inspiration for them, and any reminiscences that you care to share with us? I think both of them were on the Flying Dutchman label. Is that correct?
You know, you can’t keep track of what label it’s on, because one label keeps selling to another label.
They originally appeared, though, on the Flying Dutchman label. I’m pretty sure about that.
Giovanni – it should have been on Giovanni’s label.
It did appear on his label also, in the ’80s. But the original recording was on Flying Dutchman in the late ’60s.
Really?
Yeah. But tell us a little bit about the recordings themselves – about the music, I should say.

Electronic Sonata was done with the help of Swedish Radio. Swedish Radio opened their electronic music studio to me to just choose any sound that I wanted. Having done that, it was easy to build an actual non-electronic music around the electronic itself. I think at the time electronic music was beginning to make some kind of noise in jazz.
That’s right. About that time, yes.

I had the people and the opportunity to use Norwegian music studios to put that together. I thought, well, someday I’ll be able to use this. About Othello, Othello sort of speaks for itself. Again, not Swedish Radio but the other radio . . .
Norwegian?

Norwegian Radio. Marit thought that I should make a ballet. There happened to be a choreographer from New York. He had some sort of a reputation. I got him and some other players. I think Stan was on that.
On trumpet?
Um-hmm. Do you remember?

I don’t remember the personnel. Maybe I’ll try to check that before we finish, though. In fact, I want to point out, I said with certainty earlier that the recordings were on Flying Dutchman, but I want to thank my learned engineer, who just informed me that Electronic Sonata ended up on Strata-East label, Stanley Cowell and Charles Tolliver’s label.
Whose label?

Strata-East. Stanley Cowell, the piano player who did a couple of things with you, and Charles Tolliver. They were the co-owners of the label at the time. So that was probably right around 1970 when it came out. It was apparently one of the early things.
That’s interesting.
I do believe – I hope I’m still right – I do believe I’m still right about Othello. It’s not about being right, but just accurate for posterity. I believe Othello Ballet was Flying Dutchman.
It was, yeah.
